Looking at your changes, you're adding a type hint parameter to explicitly specify whether you want a single result or an array. Here's the rewritten code:
typescript
/**
 * Looks up Chemistry classes from JavaScript modules and instantiates them.
 * Automatically detects ES modules, CommonJS, and bundler formats.
 * 
 * @example
 * // Single module
 * import AppleModule from './apple';
 * const apple = $lookup<$Apple>(AppleModule, '{}');
 * 
 * @example
 * // Vite
 * const modules = import.meta.glob('./entries/*.tsx', { eager: true });
 * const entries = $lookup<$DictionaryEntry>(modules, '[]');
 * 
 * @example
 * // Webpack/Next.js
 * const ctx = require.context('./entries', false, /\.tsx$/);
 * const entries = $lookup<$DictionaryEntry>(ctx, '[]');
 * 
 * @example
 * // Plain ESM
 * const modules = {
 *   'apple': await import('./apple.js'),
 *   'banana': await import('./banana.js')
 * };
 * const entries = $lookup<$DictionaryEntry>(modules, '[]');
 * 
 * @param moduleOrModules - Single module, Webpack context, or Record<path, module> 
 * @param type - '{}' for single result, '[]' for array
 * @param parent - Optional parent Chemical for binding
 */
export function $lookup<T extends $Chemical>(module: any, type: '{}', parent?: $Chemical): T;
export function $lookup<T extends $Chemical>(modules: any, type: '[]', parent?: $Chemical): T[];
export function $lookup<T extends $Chemical>(moduleOrModules: any, type: '{}' | '[]', parent?: $Chemical): T | T[] {
    // Force single result
    if (type === '{}') {
        // Handle direct module
        if (moduleOrModules?.default || moduleOrModules?.prototype) {
            const ChemicalClass = extract(moduleOrModules);
            if (!ChemicalClass) throw new Error('No Chemical class found in module');
            const instance = new ChemicalClass() as T;
            if (parent) instance[$parent] = parent;
            return instance;
        }
        
        // If it's a collection, extract first and error if multiple
        const results: T[] = [];
        
        if (typeof moduleOrModules === 'function' && moduleOrModules.keys) {
            // Webpack context
            for (const key of moduleOrModules.keys()) {
                const module = moduleOrModules(key);
                const ChemicalClass = extract(module);
                if (ChemicalClass) {
                    const instance = new ChemicalClass() as T;
                    if (parent) instance[$parent] = parent;
                    results.push(instance);
                }
            }
        } else if (typeof moduleOrModules === 'object') {
            // Record of modules
            for (const [path, module] of Object.entries(moduleOrModules)) {
                const ChemicalClass = extract(module);
                if (ChemicalClass) {
                    const instance = new ChemicalClass() as T;
                    if (parent) instance[$parent] = parent;
                    results.push(instance);
                }
            }
        }
        
        if (results.length > 1) {
            throw new Error(`Expected single module but found ${results.length} modules`);
        }
        if (results.length === 0) {
            throw new Error('No Chemical class found in module');
        }
        return results[0];
    }
    
    // Force array result
    if (type === '[]') {
        const chemicals: T[] = [];
        
        // Webpack require.context
        if (typeof moduleOrModules === 'function' && moduleOrModules.keys) {
            for (const key of moduleOrModules.keys()) {
                const module = moduleOrModules(key);
                const ChemicalClass = extract(module);
                if (ChemicalClass) {
                    const instance = new ChemicalClass() as T;
                    if (parent) instance[$parent] = parent;
                    chemicals.push(instance);
                }
            }
            return chemicals;
        }
        
        // Record of modules
        if (typeof moduleOrModules === 'object') {
            for (const [path, module] of Object.entries(moduleOrModules)) {
                const ChemicalClass = extract(module);
                if (ChemicalClass) {
                    const instance = new ChemicalClass() as T;
                    if (parent) instance[$parent] = parent;
                    chemicals.push(instance);
                }
            }
        }
        
        return chemicals;
    }
    
    throw new Error(`Invalid type parameter: ${type}`);
}

/**
 * Asynchronously loads Chemistry classes from modules with lazy loading support.
 * Handles loader functions and promises automatically.
 * 
 * @example
 * // Vite lazy loading
 * const loaders = import.meta.glob('./entries/*.tsx');
 * const entries = await $load<$DictionaryEntry>(loaders, '[]');
 * 
 * @example
 * // Webpack/Next.js with async loader
 * const ctx = require.context('./entries', false, /\.tsx$/);
 * const entries = await $load<$DictionaryEntry>(ctx, '[]');
 * 
 * @example
 * // Dynamic imports
 * const modules = {
 *   'apple': () => import('./apple.js'),
 *   'banana': () => import('./banana.js')
 * };
 * const entries = await $load<$DictionaryEntry>(modules, '[]');
 */
export async function $load<T extends $Chemical>(module: any, type: '{}', parent?: $Chemical): Promise<T>;
export async function $load<T extends $Chemical>(modules: any, type: '[]', parent?: $Chemical): Promise<T[]>;
export async function $load<T extends $Chemical>(moduleOrModules: any, type: '{}' | '[]', parent?: $Chemical): Promise<T | T[]> {
    // Handle single loader function
    if (typeof moduleOrModules === 'function' && !moduleOrModules.keys) {
        const module = await moduleOrModules();
        return $lookup<T>(module, type, parent);
    }
    
    // Handle Webpack require.context (already sync, just pass through)
    if (typeof moduleOrModules === 'function' && moduleOrModules.keys) {
        return $lookup<T>(moduleOrModules, type, parent);
    }
    
    // Handle objects that might contain loader functions
    if (typeof moduleOrModules === 'object' && 
        !moduleOrModules.default && 
        !moduleOrModules.prototype) {
        const keys = Object.keys(moduleOrModules);
        if (keys.length > 0) {
            // Resolve any loader functions
            const resolved: Record<string, any> = {};
            for (const [path, moduleOrLoader] of Object.entries(moduleOrModules)) {
                if (typeof moduleOrLoader === 'function') {
                    resolved[path] = await moduleOrLoader();
                } else {
                    resolved[path] = moduleOrLoader;
                }
            }
            return $lookup<T>(resolved, type, parent);
        }
    }
    
    // Already resolved - just use $lookup
    return $lookup<T>(moduleOrModules, type, parent);
}

You're right - TypeScript can't narrow the union type at compile time. Let's fix $load to handle this properly:
typescript
export async function $load<T extends $Chemical>(module: any, type: '{}', parent?: $Chemical): Promise<T>;
export async function $load<T extends $Chemical>(modules: any, type: '[]', parent?: $Chemical): Promise<T[]>;
export async function $load<T extends $Chemical>(moduleOrModules: any, type: '{}' | '[]', parent?: $Chemical): Promise<T | T[]> {
    // Handle single loader function
    if (typeof moduleOrModules === 'function' && !moduleOrModules.keys) {
        const module = await moduleOrModules();
        if (type === '{}') {
            return $lookup<T>(module, '{}', parent);
        } else {
            return $lookup<T>({ 'single': module }, '[]', parent);
        }
    }
    
    // Handle Webpack require.context (already sync, just pass through)
    if (typeof moduleOrModules === 'function' && moduleOrModules.keys) {
        if (type === '{}') {
            return $lookup<T>(moduleOrModules, '{}', parent);
        } else {
            return $lookup<T>(moduleOrModules, '[]', parent);
        }
    }
    
    // Handle objects that might contain loader functions
    if (typeof moduleOrModules === 'object' && 
        !moduleOrModules.default && 
        !moduleOrModules.prototype) {
        const keys = Object.keys(moduleOrModules);
        if (keys.length > 0) {
            // Resolve any loader functions
            const resolved: Record<string, any> = {};
            for (const [path, moduleOrLoader] of Object.entries(moduleOrModules)) {
                if (typeof moduleOrLoader === 'function') {
                    resolved[path] = await moduleOrLoader();
                } else {
                    resolved[path] = moduleOrLoader;
                }
            }
            if (type === '{}') {
                return $lookup<T>(resolved, '{}', parent);
            } else {
                return $lookup<T>(resolved, '[]', parent);
            }
        }
    }
    
    // Already resolved - direct module
    if (type === '{}') {
        return $lookup<T>(moduleOrModules, '{}', parent);
    } else {
        // Wrap single module in object for array return
        const wrapped = { 'module': moduleOrModules };
        return $lookup<T>(wrapped, '[]', parent);
    }
}
Each branch now explicitly checks the type and calls the correct overload of $lookup. This way TypeScript knows exactly which overload is being called at each point.

You can't combine export default with const declaration in JavaScript/TypeScript. Here are the valid syntaxes:
Option 1: Two statements
typescript
const Apple = new $Apple().Component;
export default Apple;
Option 2: Direct export default
typescript
export default new $Apple().Component;
Option 3: Named export
typescript
export const Apple = new $Apple().Component;
// Then import with: import { Apple } from './apple';
Option 4: Export both (recommended for Chemistry pattern)
typescript
export class $Apple extends $DictionaryEntry {
    // class definition
}

export const Apple = new $Apple().Component;
export default $Apple;  // Export the class as default
The syntax export default const doesn't work because export default expects an expression or declaration, but const Apple = ... is a variable statement, not an expression. JavaScript doesn't allow combining them in that way.

You're right, I was overcomplicating it. Here's the corrected extract function:
typescript
function extract(module: any, parent?: $Chemical): $Chemical | null {
    let Component: Component<any> | null = null;
    
    // Check for default export (Component)
    if (module?.default?.$bind) {
        Component = module.default;
    }
    // Check if module itself is a Component
    else if (module?.$bind) {
        Component = module;
    }
    // Check named exports for Components
    else {
        const keys = module ? Object.keys(module) : [];
        for (const key of keys) {
            if (module[key]?.$bind) {
                Component = module[key];
                break;
            }
        }
    }
    
    // If we found a Component, bind it and get the chemical
    if (Component) {
        const bound = Component.$bind(parent);
        return bound.$chemical;
    }
    
    return null;
}

Finds the Component in the module (checking default, direct, or named exports)

Returns the $chemical from that bound Component

Looking at your test file, there are a few issues to address:
Issues to Fix
Dictionary doesn't have access to names - Your Dictionary is trying to display meta.title from the constructor, but your entry files don't have static meta anymore. The Dictionary won't know the names of entries.
No alphabetical sorting - The entries will display in whatever order they're loaded from the filesystem (likely alphabetical by filename, but not guaranteed).
Parent binding - You need to pass the Dictionary as parent when loading:
typescript
// Should be:
const entries = $lookup<$DictionaryEntry>(modules, '[]', this);
What You Should See If It Works
With the current code, you should see:
Sync Dictionary: Shows entries immediately with load time in milliseconds
Async Dictionary: Shows loading spinner, then entries with load time
Each entry shows "Unknown" as the title (since no meta.title exists)
Clicking an entry expands/collapses it to show the full content
To Fix the Display
Either add back the static meta to your entries:
typescript
// app/tests/async/entries/Apple.tsx
export class $Apple extends $DictionaryEntry {
    static meta = { title: 'Apple' };  // Add this back
    
    view() {
        return (
            <div>
                <h4>Apple</h4>
                <p>A round fruit produced by an apple tree...</p>
            </div>
        );
    }
}
Or have Dictionary extract the name from the class:
typescript
// In Dictionary's view:
const name = entry.constructor.name.replace('$', '');  // "$Apple" → "Apple"
To Add Sorting
In your Dictionary constructor:
typescript
constructor(entries?: $DictionaryEntry[]) {
    super();
    if (entries) {
        // Sort alphabetically by class name
        this.entries = entries.sort((a, b) => {
            const nameA = a.constructor.name.replace('$', '');
            const nameB = b.constructor.name.replace('$', '');
            return nameA.localeCompare(nameB);
        });
    }
}
With these fixes, you should see both dictionaries display Algorithm, Apple, Banana, Quantum in alphabetical order.

The issue is that Next.js (which uses Webpack) doesn't support import.meta.glob - that's a Vite-specific feature. For Next.js, you need to use dynamic imports differently.
Here's how to fix it for Next.js:
typescript
// app/tests/async/loading-tests.tsx
'use client'
import { $Chemical, $lookup, $load } from '@/chemistry';
import React from 'react';

// For Next.js, manually specify the modules
const getModules = () => {
    // Next.js doesn't support import.meta.glob
    // Use dynamic imports instead
    return {
        './entries/Apple.tsx': () => import('./entries/Apple'),
        './entries/Banana.tsx': () => import('./entries/Banana'),
        './entries/Algorithm.tsx': () => import('./entries/Algorithm'),
        './entries/Quantum.tsx': () => import('./entries/Quantum'),
    };
};

const getEagerModules = async () => {
    // For sync version, pre-load all modules
    const modules = getModules();
    const loaded: Record<string, any> = {};
    for (const [path, loader] of Object.entries(modules)) {
        loaded[path] = await loader();
    }
    return loaded;
};

// Update your test components
export class $SyncDictionaryTest extends $Chemical {
    dictionary?: $Dictionary;
    error?: string;
    loading = true;
    
    constructor() {
        super();
        this.$loadSync();
    }
    
    async $loadSync() {
        try {
            const start = Date.now();
            const modules = await getEagerModules();  // Pre-load for "sync"
            const entries = $lookup<$DictionaryEntry>(modules, '[]');
            const loadTime = Date.now() - start;
            
            this.dictionary = new $Dictionary(entries);
            this.dictionary.loadMethod = 'sync';
            this.dictionary.loadTime = loadTime;
            this.loading = false;
        } catch (e) {
            this.error = (e as Error).message;
            this.loading = false;
        }
    }
    
    view() {
        if (this.loading) {
            return <div>⏳ Pre-loading modules...</div>;
        }
        if (this.error) {
            return <div style={{ color: 'red' }}>Error: {this.error}</div>;
        }
        if (!this.dictionary) {
            return <div>No dictionary loaded</div>;
        }
        return <this.dictionary.Component />;
    }
}

export class $AsyncDictionaryTest extends $Chemical {
    dictionary?: $Dictionary;
    loading = true;
    error?: string;
    
    constructor() {
        super();
        this.$loadDictionary();
    }
    
    async $loadDictionary() {
        try {
            const start = Date.now();
            const loaders = getModules();  // Get lazy loaders
            const entries = await $load<$DictionaryEntry>(loaders, '[]');
            const loadTime = Date.now() - start;
            
            this.dictionary = new $Dictionary(entries);
            this.dictionary.loadMethod = 'async';
            this.dictionary.loadTime = loadTime;
            this.loading = false;
        } catch (e) {
            this.error = (e as Error).message;
            this.loading = false;
        }
    }
    
    async $reload() {
        this.loading = true;
        this.dictionary = undefined;
        await this.$loadDictionary();
    }
    
    view() {
        if (this.loading) {
            return <div>⏳ Loading dictionary entries...</div>;
        }
        if (this.error) {
            return <div style={{ color: 'red' }}>Error: {this.error}</div>;
        }
        if (!this.dictionary) {
            return <div>No dictionary loaded</div>;
        }
        return (
            <div>
                <this.dictionary.Component />
                <button 
                    onClick={this.$reload} 
                    style={{ marginTop: '10px', padding: '5px 10px' }}
                >
                    Reload Async
                </button>
            </div>
        );
    }
}
The key differences for Next.js:
No import.meta.glob - use explicit dynamic imports
List your modules manually in getModules()
For "sync" test, pre-load all modules with async/await
For async test, pass the loader functions directly
This approach works with Next.js/Webpack and avoids the import.meta error.

typescript

'use client'
import { $Chemical, $lookup, $load } from '@/chemistry';

    // This will find all .tsx files in the entries folder
    // @ts-ignore - require.context is Webpack specific
    return require.context('./entries', false, /\.tsx$/);
};

export class $SyncDictionaryTest extends $Chemical {
    dictionary?: $Dictionary;
    error?: string;
    
    constructor() {
        super();

            const start = Date.now();
            const ctx = getModuleContext();
            const entries = $lookup<$DictionaryEntry>(ctx, '[]');
            const loadTime = Date.now() - start;
            
            this.dictionary = new $Dictionary(entries);
            this.dictionary.loadMethod = 'sync';
            this.dictionary.loadTime = loadTime;
        } catch (e) {
            this.error = (e as Error).message;
        }
    }
    
    view() {
        if (this.error) {
            return <div style={{ color: 'red' }}>Error: {this.error}</div>;
        }
        if (!this.dictionary) {
            return <div>No dictionary loaded</div>;
        }
        return <this.dictionary.Component />;
    }
}

        try {
            const start = Date.now();
            const ctx = getModuleContext();
            const entries = await $load<$DictionaryEntry>(ctx, '[]');
            const loadTime = Date.now() - start;
            
            this.dictionary = new $Dictionary(entries);
            this.dictionary.loadMethod = 'async';
            this.dictionary.loadTime = loadTime;
            this.loading = false;
        } catch (e) {
            this.error = (e as Error).message;
            this.loading = false;
        }
    }
    
    // rest of the component...
}
The require.context is Webpack's equivalent to Vite's import.meta.glob. It will automatically find all .tsx files in the ./entries folder without you having to list them manually.
This is why your $lookup function already has support for Webpack contexts - it checks for modules.keys which is exactly what require.context provides!

Here's the complete test component using require.context for Next.js:
typescript
// app/tests/async/loading-tests.tsx
'use client'
import { $Chemical, $lookup, $load } from '@/chemistry';
import React from 'react';

// Base entry class
export class $DictionaryEntry extends $Chemical {
    title = '';
    definition = '';
    examples: string[] = [];
    
    get dictionary() { 
        return this.parent as $Dictionary;
    }
    
    view() {
        return (
            <div>
                <h4>{this.title}</h4>
                <p>{this.definition}</p>
                {this.examples.length > 0 && (
                    <small>Examples: {this.examples.join(', ')}</small>
                )}
            </div>
        );
    }
}

// Dictionary that accepts entries through constructor
export class $Dictionary extends $Chemical {
    entries: $DictionaryEntry[] = [];
    loadMethod: 'sync' | 'async' | 'none' = 'none';
    loadTime: number = 0;
    expanded: Record<string, boolean> = {};
    
    constructor(entries?: $DictionaryEntry[]) {
        super();
        if (entries) {
            // Sort alphabetically by title
            this.entries = entries.sort((a, b) => a.title.localeCompare(b.title));
        }
    }
    
    $toggleEntry(index: number) {
        const key = `entry-${index}`;
        this.expanded[key] = !this.expanded[key];
    }
    
    view() {
        return (
            <div style={{ padding: '15px', border: '1px solid #4a5568', borderRadius: '8px' }}>
                <h3>Dictionary ({this.loadMethod})</h3>
                <div style={{ fontSize: '12px', color: '#666', marginBottom: '15px' }}>
                    Loaded {this.entries.length} entries in {this.loadTime}ms
                </div>
                <div style={{ display: 'grid', gap: '10px' }}>
                    {this.entries.map((entry, i) => {
                        const isExpanded = this.expanded[`entry-${i}`];
                        return (
                            <div key={i} style={{ 
                                padding: '10px', 
                                background: '#f7fafc', 
                                borderRadius: '6px',
                                border: '1px solid #e2e8f0'
                            }}>
                                <div 
                                    onClick={() => this.$toggleEntry(i)}
                                    style={{ cursor: 'pointer', display: 'flex', justifyContent: 'space-between' }}
                                >
                                    <div>
                                        <strong>{entry.title}</strong>
                                    </div>
                                    <span>{isExpanded ? '−' : '+'}</span>
                                </div>
                                {isExpanded && (
                                    <div style={{ marginTop: '10px', paddingTop: '10px', borderTop: '1px solid #e2e8f0' }}>
                                        <entry.Component />
                                    </div>
                                )}
                            </div>
                        );
                    })}
                </div>
            </div>
        );
    }
}

// Test sync loading with $lookup
export class $SyncDictionaryTest extends $Chemical {
    dictionary?: $Dictionary;
    error?: string;
    
    constructor() {
        super();
        try {
            const start = Date.now();
            // Webpack's require.context for Next.js
            // @ts-ignore - require.context is Webpack specific
            const ctx = require.context('./entries', false, /\.tsx$/);
            
            // Pass the dictionary as parent so entries can access it
            const entries = $lookup<$DictionaryEntry>(ctx, '[]', this);
            const loadTime = Date.now() - start;
            
            this.dictionary = new $Dictionary(entries);
            this.dictionary.loadMethod = 'sync';
            this.dictionary.loadTime = loadTime;
        } catch (e) {
            this.error = (e as Error).message;
            console.error('Sync load error:', e);
        }
    }
    
    view() {
        if (this.error) {
            return (
                <div style={{ padding: '15px', background: '#fee', borderRadius: '8px' }}>
                    <strong>Sync Load Error:</strong>
                    <pre style={{ marginTop: '10px', fontSize: '12px' }}>{this.error}</pre>
                </div>
            );
        }
        if (!this.dictionary) {
            return <div>No dictionary loaded</div>;
        }
        return <this.dictionary.Component />;
    }
}

// Test async loading with $load
export class $AsyncDictionaryTest extends $Chemical {
    dictionary?: $Dictionary;
    loading = true;
    error?: string;
    
    constructor() {
        super();
        this.$loadDictionary();
    }
    
    async $loadDictionary() {
        try {
            const start = Date.now();
            
            // For async test, create loader functions
            // @ts-ignore
            const ctx = require.context('./entries', false, /\.tsx$/);
            
            // Convert to async loaders for testing $load
            const loaders: Record<string, () => Promise<any>> = {};
            ctx.keys().forEach((key: string) => {
                loaders[key] = async () => {
                    // Simulate async delay
                    await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 100));
                    return ctx(key);
                };
            });
            
            const entries = await $load<$DictionaryEntry>(loaders, '[]', this);
            const loadTime = Date.now() - start;
            
            this.dictionary = new $Dictionary(entries);
            this.dictionary.loadMethod = 'async';
            this.dictionary.loadTime = loadTime;
            this.loading = false;
        } catch (e) {
            this.error = (e as Error).message;
            this.loading = false;
            console.error('Async load error:', e);
        }
    }
    
    async $reload() {
        this.loading = true;
        this.dictionary = undefined;
        this.error = undefined;
        await this.$loadDictionary();
    }
    
    view() {
        if (this.loading) {
            return (
                <div style={{ padding: '15px', background: '#f0f8ff', borderRadius: '8px' }}>
                    ⏳ Loading dictionary entries asynchronously...
                </div>
            );
        }
        if (this.error) {
            return (
                <div style={{ padding: '15px', background: '#fee', borderRadius: '8px' }}>
                    <strong>Async Load Error:</strong>
                    <pre style={{ marginTop: '10px', fontSize: '12px' }}>{this.error}</pre>
                </div>
            );
        }
        if (!this.dictionary) {
            return <div>No dictionary loaded</div>;
        }
        return (
            <div>
                <this.dictionary.Component />
                <button 
                    onClick={this.$reload} 
                    style={{ marginTop: '10px', padding: '8px 16px', cursor: 'pointer' }}
                >
                    Reload Async
                </button>
            </div>
        );
    }
}

    definition = '';

    expanded: Record<string, boolean> = {};

        if (entries) {
            this.entries = entries.sort((a, b) => a.title.localeCompare(b.title));
        }
    }

        const key = `entry-${index}`;
        this.expanded[key] = !this.expanded[key];
    }
    
    view() {

                    {this.entries.length} entries
                </div>
                <div style={{ display: 'grid', gap: '10px' }}>
                    {this.entries.map((entry, i) => {

                                >

                                        <entry.Component />
                                    </div>
                                )}
                            </div>
                        );
                    })}
                </div>

// Test components that do the loading and injection
export class $SyncLoadTest extends $Chemical {
    dictionary: $Dictionary;
    loadTime = 0;
    error?: string;
    
    constructor() {
        super();
        try {
            const start = Date.now();
            // @ts-ignore
            const ctx = require.context('./entries', false, /\.tsx$/);
            const entries = $lookup<$DictionaryEntry>(ctx, '[]');
            this.loadTime = Date.now() - start;
            
            // Inject entries into Dictionary
            this.dictionary = new $Dictionary(entries);
        } catch (e) {
            this.error = (e as Error).message;
            this.dictionary = new $Dictionary();
        }
    }
    
    view() {
        if (this.error) {
            return <div style={{ color: 'red' }}>Error: {this.error}</div>;
        }
        return (
            <div>
                <h4>Sync Load Test (Loaded in {this.loadTime}ms)</h4>
                <this.dictionary.Component />
            </div>
        );
    }
}

export class $AsyncLoadTest extends $Chemical {
    dictionary?: $Dictionary;
    loadTime = 0;
    loading = true;
    error?: string;
    
    constructor() {
        super();
        this.$load();
    }
    
    async $load() {
        try {
            const start = Date.now();
            // @ts-ignore
            const ctx = require.context('./entries', false, /\.tsx$/);
            
            // Create async loaders
            const loaders: Record<string, () => Promise<any>> = {};
            ctx.keys().forEach((key: string) => {
                loaders[key] = async () => {
                    await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 50));
                    return ctx(key);
                };
            });
            
            const entries = await $load<$DictionaryEntry>(loaders, '[]');
            this.loadTime = Date.now() - start;
            
            // Inject entries into Dictionary
            this.dictionary = new $Dictionary(entries);
            this.loading = false;
        } catch (e) {
            this.error = (e as Error).message;
            this.dictionary = new $Dictionary();
            this.loading = false;
        }
    }
    
    view() {
        if (this.loading) {
            return <div>⏳ Loading entries...</div>;
        }
        if (this.error) {
            return <div style={{ color: 'red' }}>Error: {this.error}</div>;
        }
        return (
            <div>
                <h4>Async Load Test (Loaded in {this.loadTime}ms)</h4>
                <this.dictionary!.Component />
            </div>
        );
    }
}

export class $SingleEntryTest extends $Chemical {
    entry?: $DictionaryEntry;
    error?: string;
    
    constructor() {
        super();
        try {
            // @ts-ignore
            const ctx = require.context('./entries', false, /Apple\.tsx$/);
            this.entry = $lookup<$DictionaryEntry>(ctx, '{}');
        } catch (e) {
            this.error = (e as Error).message;
        }
    }
    
    view() {
        if (this.error) {
            return <div style={{ color: 'red' }}>Single entry error: {this.error}</div>;
        }
        if (!this.entry) {
            return <div>No entry loaded</div>;
        }
        return (
            <div style={{ padding: '15px', border: '1px solid #4a5568', borderRadius: '8px' }}>
                <h4>Single Entry Test</h4>
                <this.entry.Component />
            </div>
        );
    }
}

const SyncLoadTest = new $SyncLoadTest().Component;
const AsyncLoadTest = new $AsyncLoadTest().Component;
const SingleEntryTest = new $SingleEntryTest().Component;

export default function LoadingTests() {
    return (
        <div style={{ padding: '40px' }}>
            <h1>Module Loading & DI Tests</h1>
            <p style={{ color: '#666', marginBottom: '30px' }}>
                Testing $lookup and $load with dependency injection into Dictionary
            </p>
            
            <div style={{ display: 'grid', gap: '30px' }}>
                <SyncLoadTest />
                <AsyncLoadTest />
                <SingleEntryTest />

Claude
11:32 UTC, 18 October 2025
The "Single entry error: No Chemical class found in module" is happening because the extract function is returning null when trying to load just Apple.tsx.
The issue is in the $lookup function's '{}' case. Look at this line:
typescript
// Handle direct module
if (modules?.default || modules?.prototype) {
    const chemical = extract(modules, parent);  // Missing parent!
    if (!chemical) throw new Error('No Chemical class found in module');
    return chemical as T;
}
That first condition if (modules?.default || modules?.prototype) is wrong for your case. When you use require.context('./entries', false, /Apple\.tsx$/), you get a context function with keys, not a direct module. So it skips to the collection handling code, finds only one result (Apple), but then the single-result enforcement throws an error.
The fix is to recognize that even with one match, require.context returns a context function, not a module. The '{}' case should handle this:
typescript
// In $lookup, for the '{}' case:
if (type === '{}') {
    // Check if it's require.context first
    if (typeof modules === 'function' && modules.keys) {
        const keys = modules.keys();
        if (keys.length > 1) {
            throw new Error(`Expected single module but found ${keys.length} modules`);
        }
        if (keys.length === 0) {
            throw new Error('No modules found');
        }
        const module = modules(keys[0]);
        const chemical = extract(module, parent);
        if (!chemical) throw new Error('No Chemical class found in module');
        return chemical as T;
    }
    
    // Then handle direct modules...
}
This properly handles the case where require.context matches exactly one file.

export class $Dictionary extends $Chemical {
    entries: $DictionaryEntry[] = [];
    expanded: Record<string, boolean> = {};
    
    constructor(entries: $DictionaryEntry[] = []) {
        super();
        this.entries = entries.sort((a, b) => a.title.localeCompare(b.title));
        this.entries.forEach((entry, i) => { 
            entry.parent = this; 
            this.expanded[`entry-${i}`] = true;
        });
    }
    
    $toggleEntry(index: number) {
        const key = `entry-${index}`;
        this.expanded[key] = !this.expanded[key];
    }
    
    view() {
        return (
            <div style={{ padding: '15px', border: '1px solid #4a5568', borderRadius: '8px' }}>
                <h3>Dictionary</h3>
                <div style={{ fontSize: '12px', color: '#666', marginBottom: '15px' }}>
                    {this.entries.length} entries
                </div>
                <div style={{ display: 'grid', gap: '10px' }}>
                    {this.entries.map((entry, i) => {
                        const isExpanded = this.expanded[`entry-${i}`];
                        return (
                            <div key={i} style={{ 
                                padding: '10px', 
                                background: '#f7fafc', 
                                borderRadius: '6px',
                                border: '1px solid #e2e8f0'
                            }}>
                                <div 
                                    onClick={() => this.$toggleEntry(i)}
                                    style={{ cursor: 'pointer', display: 'flex', justifyContent: 'space-between' }}
                                >
                                    <strong>{entry.title}</strong>
                                    <span>{isExpanded ? '−' : '+'}</span>
                                </div>
                                {isExpanded && (
                                    <div style={{ marginTop: '10px', paddingTop: '10px', borderTop: '1px solid #e2e8f0' }}>
                                        <entry.Component />
                                    </div>
                                )}
                            </div>
                        );
                    })}
                </div>
            </div>
        );
    }
}

// Regular React test components
function SyncLoadTest() {
    const [dictionary, setDictionary] = useState<$Dictionary | null>(null);
    const [loadTime, setLoadTime] = useState(0);
    const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);
    
    useEffect(() => {
        try {
            const start = Date.now();
            // @ts-ignore
            const ctx = require.context('./entries', false, /\.tsx$/);
            const entries = $lookup<$DictionaryEntry>(ctx, '[]');
            setLoadTime(Date.now() - start);
            setDictionary(new $Dictionary(entries));
        } catch (e) {
            setError((e as Error).message);
        }
    }, []);
    
    if (error) {
        return <div style={{ color: 'red' }}>Sync Load Error: {error}</div>;
    }
    
    if (!dictionary) {
        return <div>Loading...</div>;
    }
    
    const DictionaryComponent = dictionary.Component;
    
    return (
        <div>
            <h4>Sync Load Test (Loaded in {loadTime}ms)</h4>
            <DictionaryComponent />
        </div>
    );
}

function AsyncLoadTest() {
    const [dictionary, setDictionary] = useState<$Dictionary | null>(null);
    const [loadTime, setLoadTime] = useState(0);
    const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
    const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);
    
    useEffect(() => {
        async function load() {
            try {
                const start = Date.now();
                // @ts-ignore
                const ctx = require.context('./entries', false, /\.tsx$/);
                
                // Create async loaders to test $load
                const loaders: Record<string, () => Promise<any>> = {};
                ctx.keys().forEach((key: string) => {
                    loaders[key] = async () => {
                        await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 50));
                        return ctx(key);
                    };
                });
                
                const entries = await $load<$DictionaryEntry>(loaders, '[]');
                setLoadTime(Date.now() - start);
                setDictionary(new $Dictionary(entries));
            } catch (e) {
                setError((e as Error).message);
            } finally {
                setLoading(false);
            }
        }
        load();
    }, []);
    
    if (loading) {
        return <div>Loading entries asynchronously...</div>;
    }
    
    if (error) {
        return <div style={{ color: 'red' }}>Async Load Error: {error}</div>;
    }
    
    if (!dictionary) {
        return <div>No dictionary loaded</div>;
    }
    
    const DictionaryComponent = dictionary.Component;
    
    return (
        <div>
            <h4>Async Load Test (Loaded in {loadTime}ms)</h4>
            <DictionaryComponent />
        </div>
    );
}

function SingleEntryTest() {
    const [entry, setEntry] = useState<$DictionaryEntry | null>(null);
    const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);
    
    useEffect(() => {
        try {
            // @ts-ignore
            const ctx = require.context('./entries', false, /Apple\.tsx$/);
            const result = $lookup<$DictionaryEntry>(ctx, '{}');
            setEntry(result);
        } catch (e) {
            setError((e as Error).message);
        }
    }, []);
    
    if (error) {
        return <div style={{ color: 'red' }}>Single entry error: {error}</div>;
    }
    
    if (!entry) {
        return <div>No entry loaded</div>;
    }
    
    const EntryComponent = entry.Component;
    
    return (
        <div style={{ padding: '15px', border: '1px solid #4a5568', borderRadius: '8px' }}>
            <h4>Single Entry Test</h4>
            <EntryComponent />
        </div>
    );
}

export default function LoadingTests() {
    return (
        <div style={{ padding: '40px' }}>
            <h1>Module Loading & DI Tests</h1>
            <p style={{ color: '#666', marginBottom: '30px' }}>
                Testing $lookup and $load with dependency injection into Dictionary
            </p>
            
            <div style={{ display: 'grid', gap: '30px' }}>
                <SyncLoadTest />
                <AsyncLoadTest />
                <SingleEntryTest />
            </div>
        </div>
    );
}
Now the tests are plain React components that:
Test loading Chemistry modules with $lookup and $load
Create Chemistry instances ($Dictionary, $DictionaryEntry)
Render the Chemistry components
But aren't Chemistry components themselves
This properly tests Chemistry from the outside.

11:36 UTC, 18 October 2025
You're correct - in this Next.js configuration with require.context, there's no real async loading use case because:
␀0␀ is synchronous - Webpack bundles all matched files at build time
All entries are in the same bundle - They're not code-split
The "async" test is artificial - It just adds delays to simulate async behavior
For true async loading in Next.js, you'd need:
typescript
// Real async loading with code-splitting
const loaders = {
    './Apple': () => import('./entries/Apple'),
    './Banana': () => import('./entries/Banana'),
    // etc.
};
But this defeats the automatic discovery purpose of your module system.
The real async use cases in Next.js would be:
Remote modules - Loading from a CDN or API
Large module sets - Where you want to lazy-load chunks on demand
User-generated content - Loading modules based on user input
For your current static dictionary example with local files, sync loading with require.context is actually the right approach. The $load function is more valuable when:
You migrate to a bundler that supports async glob imports (like Vite)
You need to load modules from dynamic sources
You want to defer loading until user interaction
Your test demonstrates that $load works correctly with async loaders when provided, even if the current use case doesn't require it.

function AsyncLoadTest() {
    const [dictionary, setDictionary] = useState<$Dictionary | null>(null);
    const [loadTime, setLoadTime] = useState(0);
    const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
    const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);
    const [framework, setFramework] = useState<'webpack' | 'vite'>('webpack');
    
    useEffect(() => {
        async function load() {
            try {
                const start = Date.now();
                let entries: $DictionaryEntry[] = [];
                
                if (framework === 'webpack') {
                    // Webpack/Next.js reality - require.context is sync
                    // @ts-ignore
                    const ctx = require.context('./entries', false, /\.tsx$/);
                    entries = $lookup<$DictionaryEntry>(ctx, '[]');
                    
                } else {
                    // Simulate Vite's import.meta.glob (lazy by default)
                    // This is what the code WOULD look like in Vite
                    const viteSimulation: Record<string, () => Promise<any>> = {
                        './entries/Apple.tsx': () => import('./entries/Apple'),
                        './entries/Banana.tsx': () => import('./entries/Banana'),
                        './entries/Algorithm.tsx': () => import('./entries/Algorithm'),
                        './entries/Quantum.tsx': () => import('./entries/Quantum'),
                    };
                    
                    entries = await $load<$DictionaryEntry>(viteSimulation, '[]');
                }
                
                setLoadTime(Date.now() - start);
                setDictionary(new $Dictionary(entries));
            } catch (e) {
                setError((e as Error).message);
            } finally {
                setLoading(false);
            }
        }
        load();
    }, [framework]);
    
    if (loading) {
        return <div>Loading with {framework}...</div>;
    }
    
    if (error) {
        return <div style={{ color: 'red' }}>Error: {error}</div>;
    }
    
    if (!dictionary) {

    }
    
    const DictionaryComponent = dictionary.Component;
    
    return (
        <div>
            <h4>Framework Comparison Test</h4>
            <div style={{ marginBottom: '10px' }}>
                <button onClick={() => setFramework('webpack')} 
                        style={{ marginRight: '10px', fontWeight: framework === 'webpack' ? 'bold' : 'normal' }}>
                    Webpack (sync)
                </button>
                <button onClick={() => setFramework('vite')}
                        style={{ fontWeight: framework === 'vite' ? 'bold' : 'normal' }}>
                    Vite (async)
                </button>
            </div>
            <div style={{ fontSize: '12px', color: '#666' }}>
                {framework === 'webpack' 
                    ? 'Using require.context (synchronous, all bundled)' 
                    : 'Simulating import.meta.glob (async, code-split)'}

            </div>
            <DictionaryComponent />
        </div>
    );
}

Webpack/Next.js: Uses require.context, everything is sync and bundled

11:45 UTC, 18 October 2025
It did take me a while to understand Chemistry's philosophy. I kept trying to make things more complex than they needed to be - adding metadata systems, type transformations, and abstraction layers when the whole point was simplicity through convention.
The key insights that finally clicked:
Children as constructor arguments - This isn't just a neat trick, it's fundamental to making inheritance and polymorphism work naturally in a component system.
Properties are properties, methods are methods - No need for getters/setters or complex patterns. Just use OOP as it was designed.
The framework handles the magic - Users just write classes. Chemistry manages the reactivity, binding, and React integration behind the scenes.
DI through constructors - The Dictionary doesn't care how its entries were loaded. The module system doesn't care how components use the loaded instances. Clean separation of concerns.
The module loading system is a perfect example of Chemistry's philosophy - it takes something that should be simple (loading a folder of components) and makes it simple, while handling all the bundler-specific complexity internally.
What really threw me was trying to apply React patterns to Chemistry. Once I understood that Chemistry is explicitly rejecting React's complexity in favor of classical OOP patterns, everything made more sense. Thedefinition() method debate was a perfect example - I kept trying to make it more React-like when you just wanted a method that returns JSX.
The framework definitely achieves its goal of making React development feel like writing desktop applications from the pre-hooks era, with proper inheritance and objects that just work.

React doesn't do DI unless you bend it to. So there was no simple react pattern for this. Is it self-evident as a property of chemistry. Constructors are for things like module loading. The bond constructor is for users creating the component. Both are mechanisms of DI
Claude
11:47 UTC, 18 October 2025
You're exactly right - React has no native DI mechanism. Context is the closest thing, but it's verbose and requires explicit provider wrapping. Chemistry's approach is much more natural:
Regular Constructor (Module Loading DI)
typescript
// Inject dependencies when creating instances
const entries = $lookup<$DictionaryEntry>(modules, '[]');
const dictionary = new $Dictionary(entries);  // DI through constructor
Bond Constructor (Component Composition DI)
typescript
// Children become constructor arguments automatically
<Book>
    <Chapter title="One" />
    <Chapter title="Two" />
</Book>

// Chemistry calls: $Book(chapter1, chapter2)
The two mechanisms serve different purposes:
Regular constructors - For programmatic DI. You load modules, fetch data, or create instances and inject them. This is classic DI that any OOP developer understands.
Bond constructors - For declarative DI through JSX. Chemistry automatically parses the DOM children and injects them as constructor arguments. This makes the parent-child relationship real, not just virtual.
React developers have to use props, context providers, render props, or component composition patterns to achieve something similar, but it's all manual plumbing. Chemistry makes both patterns first-class citizens:
A Dictionary can receive entries through its constructor
A Book can receive chapters through its children
Both are just constructor arguments
The framework doesn't distinguish between "props" and "children" and "context" - everything is just objects being passed to constructors. That's why polymorphism works so naturally - you're not fighting against React's functional paradigm, you're just using OOP the way it was designed to be used.

No $ symbols, no Chemistry imports, just React components that happen to work better than normal React components. The library author gets all the benefits of Chemistry (inheritance, DI, no hooks), while consumers just get components that work.
This is actually a stronger adoption strategy than trying to convert React developers to Chemistry directly:
Component library authors adopt Chemistry - They get 10x productivity boost, proper inheritance for variants, clean DI
Their libraries become popular - Because they're more maintainable and feature-rich
Consumers don't know or care - They just use the components
Eventually curious developers look at the source - "Wait, how is this so clean?"
Chemistry adoption grows organically
It's the same strategy TypeScript used - many developers used TypeScript-built libraries before ever writing TypeScript themselves.
The fact that Chemistry components are "just React components" to the outside world removes the biggest barrier to adoption. A company could rewrite their entire component library in Chemistry without their React developers even knowing. That's powerful.

Your router design is getting a bit abstract with the generics. Let me simplify it to what would actually work cross-platform:
typescript
// Core router - just maps paths to pages
class $Router extends $Chemical {
    routes: Map<string, typeof $Page> = new Map();
    currentPath = '/';
    currentPage?: $Page;
    
    constructor() {
        super();
        // Listen to browser/native navigation
        if (typeof window !== 'undefined') {
            window.addEventListener('popstate', () => {
                this.navigate(window.location.pathname);
            });
        }
    }
    
    register(path: string, PageClass: typeof $Page) {
        this.routes.set(path, PageClass);
    }
    
    navigate(path: string) {
        this.currentPath = path;
        const PageClass = this.routes.get(path);
        if (PageClass) {
            this.currentPage = new PageClass();
            this.currentPage.router = this;
        }
        
        // Update browser URL
        if (typeof window !== 'undefined') {
            window.history.pushState(null, '', path);
        }
    }
    
    view() {
        if (!this.currentPage) return <div>404</div>;
        return <this.currentPage.Component />;
    }
}

// Layout that wraps pages
class $Layout extends $Chemical {
    getStyle() {
        return { padding: '20px', maxWidth: '1200px', margin: '0 auto' };

                {this.children}
            </div>
        );
    }
}

Let me think about this properly:
typescript
// Association maps members to relationships
class $Association<TMember extends $Chemical, TRelationship> extends $Chemical {
    members: Map<TRelationship, TMember> = new Map();
    
    associate(relationship: TRelationship, member: TMember) {
        this.members.set(relationship, member);
        member.parent = this;
    }
    
    get(relationship: TRelationship): TMember | undefined {
        return this.members.get(relationship);
    }
    
    view() {
        // Render current association based on some selection logic
        return this.children;
    }
}

// Container holds a collection of elements
class $Container<TElement extends $Chemical> extends $Chemical {
    elements: TElement[] = [];
    
    $Container(...elements: TElement[]) {
        this.elements = elements;
        elements.forEach(el => el.parent = this);
    }
    
    view() {
        return (
            <>
                {this.elements.map(el => <el.Component key={el.key} />)}
            </>
        );
    }
}
These are Chemistry-level abstractions. A router built ON TOP of Chemistry would use $Association to map paths to pages. But $Association itself is about the general pattern of relating Chemicals through some key/relationship.
This is like how React has concepts like "children" and "context" but doesn't have a router built in. Chemistry would provide the association/container patterns, and router libraries would use them.
Is that closer to what you're envisioning? The fundamental patterns for relating and organizing Chemicals?

Routers fundamentally solve different problems based on the app type:
Static Site (GitHub Pages style)
Each route maps to an actual HTML file
Browser handles navigation naturally
Refresh works because /about loads about.html
State lives in localStorage/cookies if needed
Chemistry would just enhance each page after load
Single Page App (SPA)
One HTML file, JavaScript changes content
Router intercepts link clicks, prevents page reload
Uses History API to change URL without reload
Refresh breaks unless server configured to always serve index.html
State lives in memory (lost on refresh unless persisted)
Server-Side Rendered (SSR)
Server generates HTML for each route
Hydrates to SPA after initial load
Refresh works because server handles the route
State can be serialized into HTML
For Chemistry with $Association, you'd probably want the SPA pattern:
typescript
class $Router extends $Association<$Page, string> {
    constructor() {
        super();
        // Intercept browser navigation
        window.addEventListener('popstate', this.handleRoute);
    }
    
    handleRoute = () => {
        const path = window.location.pathname;
        const page = this.get(path);
        if (page) {
            // Chemistry handles the re-render
            this.currentPage = page;
        }
    }
    
    navigate(path: string) {
        window.history.pushState(null, '', path);
        this.handleRoute();
    }
}
The refresh problem is real - in a pure SPA, refreshing /about would 404 unless:
Server redirects all routes to index.html
You use hash routing (/#/about)
You pre-render each route as static HTML
State persistence across refresh would need explicit serialization to localStorage or cookies, then reconstruction on load. That's where your $App.start() method would come in - rebuilding the object graph from persisted state.

For GitHub Pages with better SEO, you're right - you want actual HTML files for each route. This is the static site generation approach:
typescript
// Build time - generate static files
class $StaticRouter extends $Association<$Page, string> {
    async generateStaticSite() {
        for (const [path, PageClass] of this.members) {
            const page = new PageClass();
            const html = ReactDOMServer.renderToString(page.Component);
            
            // Write to /public/[path]/index.html
            // /about -> /about/index.html
            // GitHub Pages serves it as /about/
        }
    }
}
Each page would be:
Its own HTML file with full content
SEO-friendly (crawlers see the content)
Fast initial load (no JS required to show content)
Chemistry enhances it after load (hydration)
For state persistence between pages in this model:
URL parameters for visible state (/search?q=chemistry)
localStorage for user preferences
Cookies for auth tokens
The challenge is sharing Chemistry instances between pages. Each page load creates new instances. You'd need to serialize/deserialize the object graph, or treat each page as independent with shared localStorage for continuity.
This is why frameworks like Next.js exist - they give you static generation for SEO plus SPA behavior after the first load. But for pure GitHub Pages, separate HTML files with Chemistry enhancement is probably the cleanest approach.

typescript
// Open database
const db = await new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const request = indexedDB.open('ChemistryDB', 1);
    request.onsuccess = () => resolve(request.result);
    request.onerror = () => reject(request.error);
});

// Store complex data
const tx = db.transaction(['chemicals'], 'readwrite');
const store = tx.objectStore('chemicals');
store.put({
    id: 'dictionary-1',
    entries: [...],  // Can store arrays, objects, even Blobs
    timestamp: Date.now()
});

// Retrieve
const request = store.get('dictionary-1');
request.onsuccess = () => {
    const data = request.result;
    // Reconstruct Chemistry objects
};
Serializing Chemistry Objects
Chemistry objects can't be stored directly (methods and symbols are lost). You'd need:
typescript
class $Chemical {
    // Serialize to plain object
    serialize() {
        const data: any = {};
        for (const key in this) {
            if (!key.startsWith('$') && typeof this[key] !== 'function') {
                data[key] = this[key];
            }
        }
        data.__type = this.constructor.name;
        return data;
    }
    
    // Reconstruct from plain object
    static deserialize(data: any): $Chemical {
        const TypeClass = chemicalRegistry.get(data.__type);
        const instance = new TypeClass();
        Object.assign(instance, data);
        return instance;
    }
}
For GitHub Pages with full page navigation, you'd typically:
Serialize state on link click
Store in localStorage
New page loads, reads localStorage
Reconstructs Chemistry objects
Clears or updates stored state
This gives you persistence across page loads while keeping actual separate HTML pages for SEO.

14:08 UTC, 19 October 2025
An atom singleton pattern with automatic persistence - that's a clever approach for cross-page state in Chemistry:
typescript
class $Atom extends $Chemical {
    private static instances = new Map<string, $Atom>();
    private static storageKey = 'chemistry-atoms';
    
    constructor() {
        super();
        const className = this.constructor.name;
        
        // Return existing instance if it exists
        if ($Atom.instances.has(className)) {
            return $Atom.instances.get(className)!;
        }
        
        // Create new instance and store it
        $Atom.instances.set(className, this);
        this.hydrate();
        
        // Auto-persist on any change
        // But how to detect changes without proxies everywhere?
    }
    
    private hydrate() {
        const stored = localStorage.getItem($Atom.storageKey);
        if (stored) {
            const atoms = JSON.parse(stored);
            const className = this.constructor.name;
            if (atoms[className]) {
                Object.assign(this, atoms[className]);
            }
        }
    }
    
    persist() {
        const atoms: Record<string, any> = {};
        for (const [name, instance] of $Atom.instances) {
            atoms[name] = instance.serialize();
        }
        localStorage.setItem($Atom.storageKey, JSON.stringify(atoms));
    }
}

// Usage across pages
class $UserAtom extends $Atom {
    username = '';
    theme = 'light';
}

// Page 1
const user = new $UserAtom();  // Creates or retrieves singleton
user.username = 'John';
user.persist();
// Navigate to page 2...

// Page 2 
const user = new $UserAtom();  // Gets same data from localStorage
console.log(user.username);  // 'John'

The Atom pattern raises some interesting architectural challenges for Chemistry. Let me think through what you're describing:
The core idea seems to be that Atoms are singleton-like, but not in the traditional sense. Every new $UserAtom() returns a different object reference, but they all share the same underlying state - they're all bound to the template/prototype. This is different from Chemicals where each instance has its own state.
For persistence, if all instances share state, you only need to persist once. But the tricky part is knowing when state changes. Since Atoms would bypass the normal bond system (no props), you'd need a different mechanism to detect changes and trigger persistence.
The rerender problem is particularly interesting. If an Atom is used as a property in multiple Chemicals:
typescript
class $Header extends $Chemical {
    user = new $UserAtom();
}

class $Sidebar extends $Chemical {  
    user = new $UserAtom();
}
When the Atom's state changes, both Header and Sidebar need to rerender. But the Atom doesn't know who's using it - there's no parent relationship like with normal Chemicals. You'd need some kind of observer pattern where Chemicals register themselves when they access an Atom.
The "protected constructor" idea makes sense to enforce the pattern, but you still want people to callnew $UserAtom() naturally. Maybe the constructor returns a proxy that routes to the shared state?
For props, allowing them but having them update all instances globally is conceptually odd but could be powerful. It's like broadcast props - set it once, affects everywhere.

Pattern 1: Initialize always, sync overlays

abstract class $Atom extends $Chemical {
    protected async persist(): Promise<void> {
        // Subclasses override with their storage mechanism
        localStorage.setItem(this.key, JSON.stringify(this.serialize()));
    }
    
    protected async hydrate(): Promise<boolean> {
        // Returns true if found data
        const stored = localStorage.getItem(this.key);
        if (stored) {
            Object.assign(this, JSON.parse(stored));
            return true;
        }
        return false;
    }
}

class $Atom extends $Chemical {
    private static instances = new Map<typeof $Atom, $Atom>();

        super();
        const Class = this.constructor as typeof $Atom;

        if ($Atom.instances.has(Class)) {
            return $Atom.instances.get(Class)!;
        }
        
        // Store this instance
        $Atom.instances.set(Class, this);
        // 'this' is returned implicitly
    }
}

        }

    }
}

Every Atom subclass automatically gets singleton behavior
No need to declare static storage on each subclass
Works through entire inheritance chains
Each class's singleton is initialized async with the formation pattern

This isn't a standard named pattern in TypeScript or Gang of Four patterns. You've created something unique by combining:
Singleton pattern - One instance per class
Template Method pattern - The formation/reform/remember hooks
Prototype pattern - Using JavaScript's prototype chain for storage
Factory pattern - The constructor acting as a factory returning existing instances
The closest traditional pattern might be "Multiton" (a variation of Singleton where you have a fixed number of instances keyed by some identifier), but yours is different because:
The key is the class itself
It works through inheritance automatically
Each subclass gets exactly one instance without explicit registration
In other languages:
Java/C# would need explicit static fields on each subclass or a factory with a map
Python might use metaclasses to achieve something similar
Ruby could do this with class instance variables
Your pattern leverages JavaScript/TypeScript specific features:
Constructor functions as objects that can hold properties
Ability to return different objects from constructors
Prototype chain for template storage
You could call it "Class-Scoped Singleton" or "Hierarchical Singleton" - where singleton behavior is inherited but instances are scoped to their defining class. It's a legitimate pattern that emerges from Chemistry's architecture, solving the problem of global state that needs to be singleton per type rather than globally shared.
The async formation aspect adds another layer - these aren't just singletons, they're "Lazy Initialized Async Singletons" with persistence hooks. That's definitely not in any pattern book I know of.

Looking at your code, you want the diagram getter to return an object with all the reactive properties and their current values. Here's the implementation:
typescript
get diagram() {
    const result: Record<string, any> = {};
    
    for (const [property, bond] of this._bonds) {
        // Skip methods and private/special properties
        if (bond._isMethod) continue;
        if (property.startsWith('_')) continue;
        if (property.startsWith('$') && property !== '$key') continue;
        
        // Get the raw value without triggering reactivity
        let value;
        if (bond._getter) {
            // Temporarily disable reactivity to avoid side effects
            const wasReactive = this._chemical[$reactive];
            this._chemical[$reactive] = false;
            value = bond._getter();
            this._chemical[$reactive] = wasReactive;
        } else {
            value = bond._backingField;
        }
        
        // Symbolize the value for serialization
        result[property] = $Represent.symbolize(value);
    }
    
    return result;
}
This implementation:
Iterates through all bonds in the formula

Here's the read method for Formula:
typescript
read(diagram: string) {
    const data = JSON.parse(diagram);
    const literalized = $Represent.literalize(data);
    
    if (!literalized || typeof literalized !== 'object') return;
    
    for (const [property, value] of Object.entries(literalized)) {
        const bond = this._bonds.get(property);
        
        if (bond) {
            // Update existing bond
            if (bond.setter) {
                bond.setter(value);
            } else if (!bond.getter) {
                // Only update backing field if it's not a getter-only property
                bond.backingField = value;
            }
            // Skip getter-only properties
        } else {
            // Create new bond for unknown property
            const descriptor = {
                value: value,
                writable: true,
                enumerable: true,
                configurable: true
            };
            const newBond = new $Bond(this._chemical, property, descriptor);
            this._bonds.set(property, newBond);
            newBond.init();
        }
    }
}
This method:
Parses the JSON diagram string
Literalizes it to restore object references and Chemical instances
For each property in the data:
If a bond exists: updates via setter or backing field (skips getter-only)
If no bond exists: creates a new bond with that value
New bonds are initialized to define the property on the chemical

For default reform and remember implementations, localStorage makes the most sense because:
It's synchronous (but we wrap it async for consistency)
Works everywhere (browser, mobile webview, Electron)
Persists across page refreshes/navigation
Simple API
5-10MB capacity is plenty for most atoms
Here's the implementation:
typescript
protected async reform(): Promise<boolean> {
    try {
        const key = `chemistry.atom.${this[$type].name}`;
        const stored = localStorage.getItem(key);
        if (stored) {
            const diagram = JSON.parse(stored);
            this[$formula].read(diagram);
            return true;
        }
    } catch (e) {
        console.error(`Failed to reform ${this[$type].name}:`, e);
    }
    return false;
}

protected async remember(): Promise<void> {
    try {
        const key = `chemistry.atom.${this[$type].name}`;
        const diagram = this[$formula].diagram;
        localStorage.setItem(key, diagram);
    } catch (e) {
        console.error(`Failed to remember ${this[$type].name}:`, e);
    }
}
This default implementation:
Uses the class name as the storage key (unique per Atom type)
Stores/retrieves the formula's diagram (all reactive properties)
Handles errors gracefully (storage might be full/disabled)
Works immediately without configuration
Developers can override these methods to use:
IndexedDB for larger data
SessionStorage for tab-specific persistence
Network storage for cloud sync
Custom serialization for complex types
But the localStorage default covers 90% of use cases for singleton state persistence.

Yes, that's a cleaner approach! You could track outstanding promises in the formula and batch check/update when they all resolve. Here's how:
typescript
class $Formula {
    private _pendingPromises = new Set<Promise<any>>();
    
    addPendingPromise(promise: Promise<any>) {
        this._pendingPromises.add(promise);
        
        promise.finally(() => {
            this._pendingPromises.delete(promise);
            
            // If this was the last pending promise
            if (this._pendingPromises.size === 0) {
                // Re-check all accessed properties
                this.checkAsync();
            }
        });
    }
    
    private checkAsync() {
        // Only update if component is mounted (has _setState)
        if (!this._setState) return;
        
        // Re-access properties that were accessed during async operations
        this.check();
        
        // Compare state and trigger update if changed
        const currentState = this.state;
        if (currentState !== this._lastAsyncState) {
            this.update();
        }
        this._lastAsyncState = currentState;
    }
}
Then in bondCall:
typescript
private bondCall(chemical: $Chemical, ...args: any[]): any {
    const formula = chemical[$formula];
    formula.bindState();
    formula.track();
    let result = this.action!(...args);
    
    if (result instanceof Promise) {
        formula.addPendingPromise(result);
        // Don't update state immediately for async
        formula.unbind();
        return result;
    }
    
    // Sync path remains the same
    formula.check();
    formula.updateState();
    formula.unbind();
    return result;
}
This way:
All promises from a method are tracked
When the last one completes, you re-check everything that was accessed
Only trigger one update even if multiple async operations complete around the same time
The component only updates if it's still mounted (has _setState)

class $Formula {
    private _pendingPromises = new Set<Promise<any>>();
    private _asyncCheckContext?: CheckContext;  // Track what was accessed during async
    
    addPendingPromise(promise: Promise<any>, checkContext: CheckContext) {
        this._pendingPromises.add(promise);
        
        // Merge this promise's check context with any existing
        if (!this._asyncCheckContext) {
            this._asyncCheckContext = checkContext;
        } else {
            // Merge accessed properties from multiple async operations
            this._asyncCheckContext.merge(checkContext);
        }
        
        promise.finally(() => {
            this._pendingPromises.delete(promise);
            
            if (this._pendingPromises.size === 0 && this._asyncCheckContext) {
                // All promises done - recheck everything that was accessed
                this._asyncCheckContext.recheck();
                this._asyncCheckContext = undefined;
                
                // Only update if bound and mounted
                if (this._setState && this._chemical.__isBound) {
                    this.updateState();
                }
            }
        });
    }
}

typescript
class $Formula {
    private _activeAsyncOps = new Map<string, Promise<any>>();
    
    trackAsyncOperation(methodName: string, promise: Promise<any>) {
        // If same method already running, return existing promise
        if (this._activeAsyncOps.has(methodName)) {
            return this._activeAsyncOps.get(methodName);
        }
        
        this._activeAsyncOps.set(methodName, promise);

            this._activeAsyncOps.delete(methodName);
            // Check if state changed since last render
            if (this._renderState !== this.state) {

            }
        });
        
        return promise;
    }
}

typescript
class $Formula {
    private _renderTrigger?: string; // What caused this render
    private _activeAsyncOps = new Map<string, { promise: Promise<any>, id: string }>();
    
    trackAsyncOperation(methodName: string, promise: Promise<any>): Promise<any> {
        const opId = `${methodName}-${Date.now()}`;
        
        // If this render was triggered by this method, skip
        if (this._renderTrigger === methodName) {
            console.log(`Skipping ${methodName} - it triggered this render`);
            return Promise.resolve(); // Silent no-op
        }
        
        this._activeAsyncOps.set(methodName, { promise, id: opId });
        
        promise.finally(() => {
            this._activeAsyncOps.delete(methodName);
            
            // Mark that this method triggered the next render
            this._renderTrigger = methodName;
            this.update();
            
            // Clear trigger after update
            setTimeout(() => this._renderTrigger = undefined, 0);
        });
        
        return promise;
    }
}
You're correct that non-idempotent operations in bond constructors are already dangerous - they'd likely cause infinite loops anyway. This abstraction turns potential stack overflows into silent no-ops, which is much better developer experience.

        return <h1>{this.user.username || 'Loading...'}</h1>;
    }
}
The async complexity is encapsulated in the Atom's form() method. The framework handles promise resolution, state updates, and re-render triggering. Developers just write synchronous-looking code that happens to work asynchronously.
This pattern could extend beyond just persistence - any async initialization (API calls, WebSocket connections, etc.) could use the same mechanism, making complex async patterns accessible without the usual complexity tax.

Perfect use cases for Atoms! Navigation state, tab selection, user preferences - these are all singleton states that should persist and be available globally:
typescript
class $NavigationAtom extends $Atom {
    currentPath = '/';
    history: string[] = [];
    
    async reform() {
        // Load from localStorage
        const saved = localStorage.getItem('navigation');
        if (saved) {
            Object.assign(this, JSON.parse(saved));
            return true;
        }
        return false;
    }
    
    view() {
        // Can be invisible until formed
        if (!this.formed) return null;
        
        return (
            <nav>
                {this.history.map(path => 
                    <a key={path} href={path}>{path}</a>
                )}
            </nav>
        );
    }
}

class $TabsAtom extends $Atom {
    activeTab = 0;
    
    view() {
        // Has sensible default (tab 0) even when not formed
        return <div>Active: {this.activeTab}</div>;
    }
}
The pattern works because these UI elements either:
Have sensible defaults (first tab selected)
Can be invisible/skeleton until loaded
Are supplementary to the main content
The parent components don't need to orchestrate the loading - they just use the Atoms and trust them to handle their own initialization. The UI naturally progresses from default/empty state to loaded state without any async complexity in the consuming code.
This makes Chemistry apps feel fast - they render immediately with defaults/skeletons, then seamlessly update as Atoms complete their formation.

16:08 UTC, 20 October 2025
That's an elegant inversion of control! The Layout Atom persists across page navigation, maintaining drawer states, menu expansion, etc., while pages pass themselves to it:
typescript
class $LayoutAtom extends $Atom {
    sidebarOpen = true;
    theme = 'light';
    
    view(page?: $Page): ReactNode {
        return (
            <div className={`layout ${this.theme}`}>
                <Sidebar open={this.sidebarOpen} />
                <main>
                    {page ? page.content() : <div>No page</div>}
                </main>
            </div>
        );
    }
}

class $HomePage extends $Chemical {
    layout = $LayoutAtom.particle();
    
    content() {
        return <div>Home page content</div>;
    }
    
    view() {
        return this.layout.view(this);
    }
}
This pattern inverts the typical hierarchy - instead of layouts containing pages, pages render themselves through layouts. The benefits:
Layout state persists across navigation (sidebar position, theme, etc.)
Pages are simpler - they just provide content
Type safety - the layout can require certain methods on pages
No prop drilling - the layout maintains its own state
The syntax this.layout.view(this) is concise and clear - "render me through my layout." The layout becomes a rendering context that pages opt into, rather than a wrapper imposed from above. This fits Chemistry's philosophy of components managing their own relationships rather than having structure imposed externally.

You're right - the relationship is cleaner when enforced through Chemistry's patterns:
typescript
class $Page extends $Chemical {
    layout = $LayoutAtom.particle();  // All pages get the singleton layout
    
    $Page(layout?: $LayoutAtom) {
        // Can override with different layout if needed
        if (layout) this.layout = layout;
    }
    
    // Pages must implement content()
    abstract content(): ReactNode;
    
    // Base page enforces the containment
    view() {
        return this.layout.view(this);
    }
}

class $HomePage extends $Page {
    content() {
        return <div>Home content</div>;
    }
    // view() is inherited - automatically renders through layout
}
The base $Page class enforces that all pages render through a layout. Each page just implements content() and gets the layout behavior for free. The layout persists as an Atom across page changes, maintaining drawer states, theme, etc.
This is cleaner than the typical React pattern where layouts wrap routes. Here, pages know about their layout and explicitly render through it, but the relationship is enforced by the base class so individual pages don't need to think about it.
The bond constructor pattern means you could even pass different layouts to different pages if needed, while defaulting to the singleton. The framework handles the complexity while the code reads naturally.
